# From question to model {#sec-questions}

## Why a chapter about questions in a book about code {#sec-why-questions}

No amount of statistical sophistication rescues a badly posed question. The right
order is: question → design → data → model → inference. Tools like Julia act on the
last two steps, and are useless if the first two fail.

This chapter exists to join the book's two halves: the question you ask determines the
model structure that appears in @sec-linear-models and @sec-glm.

## Multiple working hypotheses {#sec-hypotheses}

This section will be built on @chamberlin1890method, which argued for holding several
rival hypotheses in play at once rather than defending a single one — an 1890 argument
that remains the best available description of what separates a productive question
from a defensive one.

To develop:

- Observation, pattern and process: the three levels, and why conflating them yields
  models that answer a different question than the one asked.
- Mechanistic versus phenomenological hypotheses, and what each licenses you to
  conclude.

## Design and dependence structure {#sec-design}

This section will be built on @hurlbert1984pseudoreplication, which named
pseudoreplication and catalogued its forms, and on @zuur2009mixed, whose treatment of
dependence structure connects directly to the random effects used in this book.

To develop:

- Sampling unit, experimental unit, and why the distinction sets the denominator of
  your test.
- How design structure translates into `(1 | group)` terms — the direct link to
  @sec-mixed-models.
- Effect size and power before collection, not after.

## Computation-limited questions {#sec-julia-questions}

A section specific to this book. Some ecological questions are limited by computation
rather than by data: null models with many permutations, individual-based simulation,
fitting mechanistic models by optimization. These benefit most from the language, for
the reasons discussed in @sec-why-julia.

This section needs to be written with runnable examples, like the rest of the book —
not with unverified performance claims.

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Write your project's central question in one sentence, without statistical jargon.
2. Sketch the model it implies *before* looking at the data: what response, what
   predictors, what grouping structure?
3. Identify the experimental unit in your design. How many true replicates do you
   have — not how many measurements?
